paragraphs.heading: The science of Earth
paragraphs.text: Geology is the natural science of Earth and other bodies in space: the rocks they are made of and the processes that change them over time. Its name joins two Ancient Greek words, one meaning earth and one meaning study. It describes the structure of Earth both at and below the surface and how that structure came to be. Today it overlaps heavily with the other Earth sciences, such as hydrology, and is tied into Earth system science and planetary science.

paragraphs.heading: Reading Earth's history
paragraphs.text: Geologists look at the minerals in rocks to learn how those rocks formed. Geology works out the relative ages of rocks in a place, while geochemistry, one of its branches, finds their absolute ages. By combining tools from the study of rocks, crystals and fossils, geologists can tell the story of Earth as a whole, including how old it is. Geology also supplies evidence for plate tectonics, for the history of life and for Earth's past climates.

paragraphs.heading: Methods and uses
paragraphs.text: The methods range from fieldwork and describing rocks to geophysics, chemical analysis, physical experiments and numerical models. Even meteorites are studied this way. The practical payoff is large: geology guides the search for minerals and hydrocarbons, the assessment of water supplies, the understanding of natural hazards and the clean-up of environmental damage. It is central to geological engineering and important in geotechnical engineering.

paragraphs.heading: Telling minerals apart
paragraphs.text: Minerals are naturally occurring elements and compounds with a fixed, uniform chemical make-up and atoms arranged in an orderly way. Geologists identify them with simple tests. Streak is the colour left when a sample is scratched across a porcelain plate. Hardness is how well it resists scratching, and luster describes how light reflects off it. Some tests are even more hands-on: a drop of hydrochloric acid may make a mineral fizz, and halite tastes like table salt.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds of rock
paragraphs.text: A rock is any natural solid mass or cluster of minerals or mineraloids. Most geological research centres on rocks, because they hold the main record of Earth's past. There are three major types. Igneous rock solidifies from molten magma or lava; sedimentary rock forms when rock is weathered and eroded, laid down again and hardened; and metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change the minerals of igneous or sedimentary rock. Any of the three can melt again into new magma, and the rock cycle shows how they are linked.

paragraphs.heading: Sediments and loose ground
paragraphs.text: Sedimentary rocks fall into four main groups: sandstone, shale, carbonate and evaporite. The first two are sorted mostly by grain size, the last two by their minerals and how they formed. Coal, oil and natural gas are linked mainly to sedimentary rocks rich in organic matter. Geologists also study the loose material lying on top of solid bedrock, a field often called Quaternary geology after the most recent period of geologic time.
